body.statement: For every admissible radius triple \( (r_{0n},r_{1n},r_{en})\in[0,\bar r]^3 \) for which \(\mathcal M_n\) is nonempty, the handle \(\mathfrak H_{\mathrm{lb}}\) yields constants \(c>0\) and \(\delta_0\in(0,1/4)\), uniform in \(n\), such that every rule \(T\in\mathcal T_n\), including every rule using \(O^{(n)}\), \(m_0\), \(m_1\), \(p\), and the certified radii, obeys \(\sup_{(P,m_0,m_1,p)\in\mathcal M_n}P\{|T(O^{(n)},m_0,m_1,p,r_{0n},r_{1n},r_{en})-\tau(P)|\ge c\rho_n\}\ge\delta_0\). Consequently \(\mathfrak R_n^{(1)}\ge c\delta_0\rho_n\) and \(\mathfrak R_n^{(2)}\ge c\sqrt{\delta_0}\rho_n\). Every fixed-sign law used by the fuzzy mixtures, rather than merely the mixtures themselves, belongs to \(\mathcal M_n\). Each of the four subexperiment families satisfies \(E_P[(g_1(X)-g_0(X))^2]\le M\) by regression-amplitude calibration within the applicable nuisance radius or a sufficiently small fixed constant.
body.justification: The converse now constructs the perturbable reservoir atom by atom and proves its exact geometric tail laws, equal-cell refinements, shell slack, and fixed-sign membership before applying the four testing reductions.
body.gap: Existing fuzzy-hypothesis templates do not provide this shell-preserving atomic reservoir, the empty-treated-shell coupling, the exact \(\kappa=1\) dyadic logarithm, or the fixed-band control cancellation for the public-function ATE experiment.
body.consumer: The sharp-risk and honest-length theorems consume a fixed-sign-valid lower bound in which all four separations are realized inside the same declared class and against the full public-information decision class.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(L=1-\eta_+\).  Nonemptiness of \(\mathcal M_n\), ass:uniform-shell at \(u=\lambda_0\), and ass:right-overlap imply
\[
L>\lambda_0/2.                                                   \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, if \(L\le\lambda_0/2\), then \(e(X)\le L\) almost surely, so \(P\{\lambda_0/2<e(X)\le\lambda_0\}=0\), contrary to \(c_-\lambda_0^\kappa>0\).  Ass:positivity and the lower bound in ass:uniform-shell also force infinitely many distinct positive propensity values converging to zero; hence \(\mathcal X\) is infinite.  Every singleton of a standard Borel space is measurable, and every infinite set contains a countably infinite subset.  Therefore, for every finite \(N\), we may choose mutually distinct measurable points \(x_{j,k}\), \(j\ge0\), \(1\le k\le N\), as well as disjoint countable sets of background and completion points.

We first record the elementary testing reduction.  Let sample laws \(Q_+\) and \(Q_-\) have targets \(a_+\) and \(a_-\) with \(|a_+-a_-|\ge2d\).  The events \(\{|T-a_+|<d\}\) and \(\{|T-a_-|<d\}\) are disjoint.  From the variational definition of total variation,
\[
Q_+\{|T-a_+|\ge d\}+Q_-\{|T-a_-|\ge d\}
\ge1-\operatorname{TV}(Q_+,Q_-).                              \tag{2}
\]
The same argument applies to mixture laws.  In particular, suppose that under prior \(\theta\in\{-1,1\}\) a random target is within \(d/4\) of \(\mu_\theta\), except on an event of prior probability \(\epsilon\), that \(|\mu_+-\mu_-|=2d\), and that the two sample mixtures have total variation at most \(\gamma\).  On the target-concentration event, estimation within \(d/2\) identifies the nearer center.  Applying (2) to this test shows that one mixture has error probability at least \((1-\gamma-2\epsilon)/2\).  Since a mixture error is the average of the errors of its fixed-sign laws, at least one fixed-sign law has the same lower bound.

We next construct the reservoir demanded by def:lower-bound-handle.  Fix
\[
0<s_0<\min\{L,\lambda_0\}/4,
\qquad
\Delta=c_+-2^\kappa c_->0,                                   \tag{3}
\]
where strict positivity of \(\Delta\) follows from ass:lower-shell-richness and ass:upper-shell-richness.  Choose
\[
0<A\le \frac{\Delta}{2^{\kappa+1}}                            \tag{4}
\]
small enough for the moment calibrations below.  For \(j\ge0\), let
\[
t_j=s_0 2^{-j},
\qquad
w_j=A(1-2^{-\kappa})t_j^\kappa.                              \tag{5}
\]
For each finite \(N\), assign \(P_X\{x_{j,k}\}=w_j/N\) and \(e_0(x_{j,k})=t_j\) to the distinct active points.  Thus each level has mass \(w_j\), and every level can be split into \(N\) equal measurable cells without introducing a nonatomic-coordinate assumption.

For \(0<v\le s_0\), define \(J(v)=\min\{j\ge0:t_j\le v\}\).  Then \(v/2<t_{J(v)}\le v\), and exact summation of (5) gives
\[
\begin{split}
P_X\{e_0\le v,\ \mathrm{active}\}
 &=\sum_{j\ge J(v)}w_j
 =A t_{J(v)}^\kappa,\\
E_P[e_0(X)\mathbf 1\{e_0(X)\le v,\ \mathrm{active}\}]
 &=\sum_{j\ge J(v)}t_jw_j\\
 &=A\frac{1-2^{-\kappa}}{1-2^{-(\kappa+1)}}t_{J(v)}^{\kappa+1}.
\end{split}                                                   \tag{6}
\]
Consequently
\[
A2^{-\kappa}v^\kappa
 <P_X\{e_0\le v,\ \mathrm{active}\}\le Av^\kappa           \tag{7}
\]
and
\[
A\frac{1-2^{-\kappa}}{1-2^{-(\kappa+1)}}2^{-(\kappa+1)}v^{\kappa+1}
 <E_P[e_0\mathbf 1\{e_0\le v,\ \mathrm{active}\}]
 \le A\frac{1-2^{-\kappa}}{1-2^{-(\kappa+1)}}v^{\kappa+1}. \tag{8}
\]
These are the required tail-mass and treated-mass comparisons, with constants depending only on the fixed class constants.

The moving band is also explicit.  If \(0<s\le s_0/2\), choose \(j(s)\) so that \(t_{j(s)}\le s<t_{j(s)-1}\).  Then
\(t_{j(s)-1}\in(s,2s]\), so
\[
B_s=\{s<e_0\le2s,\ \mathrm{active}\}
\quad\hbox{contains level }j(s)-1,
\quad
P_X(B_s)\ge w_{j(s)-1}\asymp s^\kappa.                       \tag{9}
\]
It contains at most two adjacent dyadic levels, so (7) also gives \(P_X(B_s)\lesssim s^\kappa\).  For the fixed control band choose any \(j_c\ge1\), put \(s_c=t_{j_c+1}\), and define
\[
B=\{s_c<e_0\le2s_c,\ \mathrm{active}\}
  =\{x_{j_c,k}:1\le k\le N\},
\qquad
m_*:=P_X(B)=w_{j_c}>0.                                      \tag{10}
\]
Thus \(B\) consists of exactly \(N\) cells of mass \(m_*/N\).

For completeness, we spell out the untouched shell allocation.  Choose \(a\in(\lambda_0/2,\min\{L,\lambda_0\}]\).  Put one background atom at \(a\) of mass \(c_-\lambda_0^\kappa\), and, for \(j\ge1\), put a background atom at \(a_j=a2^{-j}\) of mass \(c_-a_{j-1}^\kappa\).  If \(u\in[a,\lambda_0]\), exactly the top atom is in \((u/2,u]\); if \(u\in[a_j,a_{j-1})\), exactly the atom at \(a_j\) is in that shell.  Hence, at every \(0<u\le\lambda_0\),
\[
c_-u^\kappa
\le P_X\{u/2<e_0\le u,\ \mathrm{background}\}
\le2^\kappa c_-u^\kappa.                                  \tag{11}
\]
Moreover, ass:lower-shell-richness yields
\[
c_-\lambda_0^\kappa+
\frac{c_-a^\kappa}{1-2^{-\kappa}}
\le \frac{1-2^{-\kappa}}4+\frac14<\frac12.                 \tag{12}
\]
Place the remaining probability on disjoint unperturbed completion points.  At scales below \(4s_0\) these points are chosen above the shell, while at the finitely many higher scales they are filled recursively inside the unused upper-shell capacities.  This recursion is feasible because (11) uses at most \(2^\kappa c_-u^\kappa\), the active allocation reserves at most \(A(2u)^\kappa\), (4) leaves positive upper slack, and ass:upper-shell-richness supplies total high-scale capacity; the completion is never perturbed.  Thus the baseline is a probability law, the completion plus background satisfies the two shell inequalities whenever the active points are absent, and (11) supplies the lower shell bound whenever active points can enter.  All three sets of points are disjoint, so this completion changes neither (6)--(10) nor any equal-cell mass.

Now let a fixed-sign perturbation act only on the active points and satisfy \(e/e_0\in[1/2,2]\).  Then
\[
\{u/2<e\le u,\ \mathrm{active}\}
\subseteq\{e_0\le2u,\ \mathrm{active}\},
\]
and (6), including the case \(2u>s_0\) by the total mass \(As_0^\kappa\), gives
\[
P_X\{u/2<e\le u,\ \mathrm{active}\}
\le A(2u)^\kappa
\le\frac{\Delta}{2}u^\kappa.                              \tag{13}
\]
Together with (11) and the unperturbed high-scale completion, this proves, for every fixed sign rather than only after mixing,
\[
c_-u^\kappa\le P_X\{u/2<e\le u\}
\le\left(2^\kappa c_-+\frac\Delta2\right)u^\kappa
<c_+u^\kappa.                                                \tag{14}
\]
The treated fuzzy ratios \([4/5,4/3]\), the control fuzzy ratios \([3/4,5/4]\), and the unchanged families all satisfy the premise used in (13).

In every subexperiment below, draw \(D\mid X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(e(X))\), draw \((Y_0,Y_1)\) conditionally independently of \(D\) given \(X\), and put \(Y=DY_1+(1-D)Y_0\).  This verifies ass:ignorability and ass:consistency.  In the treated mean-shift families take \(Y_1=g_1(X)+\sigma Z\), where \(Z\sim N(0,1)\) is conditionally independent and \(0<\sigma^2\le\sigma_1^2\wedge M_Y/4\); elsewhere residual noise is zero.  Multiply every displayed regression amplitude and every small propensity tilt by a fixed \(c_A>0\).  Since \(r_{0n},r_{1n},r_{en}\le\bar r\), we may choose \(c_A\), depending only on the fixed class constants, so that
\[
c_A\le\min\{1/2,s_c\},
\qquad
E_P[(g_1(X)-g_0(X))^2]\le M,
\qquad
E_P[Y^2]\le M_Y                                             \tag{15}
\]
in all families.  The calculations below show that every squared regression norm is bounded by a fixed multiple of \(c_A^2\bar r^2\) or \(c_A^2\), while each treated weighted second moment is bounded by a fixed multiple of the same quantities plus \(\sigma^2\).  Thus (15) is a genuine uniform calibration, and ass:treated-residual-variance and ass:control-residual-variance hold by the chosen residual laws.

We now prove the four testing obstructions.  First, the parametric floor is obtained on two unperturbed completion points having the same fixed interior propensity and fixed positive masses.  Set the known treatment-effect signal to \(+c_A\) on one point and \(-c_A\) on the other, take the public nuisances equal to the truth, and transfer mass \(c_A/\sqrt n\) between the points in opposite directions.  The propensity distribution, hence every shell probability, is unchanged.  Direct expansion of the categorical log likelihood gives one-row Kullback--Leibler divergence at most \(C c_A^2/n\), so the product divergence is at most \(Cc_A^2\).  The inequality
\[
\operatorname{TV}(Q,Q')^2\le\frac12\operatorname{KL}(Q,Q') \tag{16}
\]
follows by integrating the pointwise convex inequality for the likelihood ratio and applying Cauchy--Schwarz.  Decreasing \(c_A\) makes product total variation at most \(1/4\), whereas the ATE separation is a fixed multiple of \(n^{-1/2}\).  Equation (2) proves the root-\(n\) obstruction.

Suppose next that \(0<\kappa<1\), \(r_{1n}>0\), and \(s=(nr_{1n}^2)^{-1}\le s_0\).  On \(A_s=\{e_0\le s,\ \mathrm{active}\}\), let \(m_s=P_X(A_s)\), set
\[
m_1=0,\quad p=e_0,\quad g_{1,\pm}=\pm h\mathbf 1_{A_s},
\quad h=\frac{c_A r_{1n}}{\sqrt{m_s}},
\quad g_0=m_0=0.                                             \tag{17}
\]
Then \(\|m_1-g_{1,\pm}\|_2=c_A r_{1n}\le r_{1n}\).  By (7)--(8), \(m_s\asymp s^\kappa\) and \(E[e_0\mathbf1_{A_s}]\asymp s^{\kappa+1}\lesssim sm_s\).  The log likelihood ratio between two normals of common variance \(\sigma^2\) and means \(h\) and \(-h\) has expectation \(2h^2/\sigma^2\).  Only treated rows in \(A_s\) differ, and therefore
\[
\operatorname{KL}(P_+^n,P_-^n)
=\frac{2nh^2}{\sigma^2}E[e_0(X)\mathbf1_{A_s}]
\le Cnh^2sm_s=Cc_A^2.                                       \tag{18}
\]
After decreasing \(c_A\), (16) and (2) apply, while
\[
|\tau(P_+)-\tau(P_-)|=2hm_s
\asymp r_{1n}s^{\kappa/2}
=n^{-\kappa/2}r_{1n}^{1-\kappa}.                            \tag{19}
\]
If \((nr_{1n}^2)^{-1}>s_0\), then \(\sqrt n r_{1n}<s_0^{-1/2}\), so the right side of (19) is at most \(s_0^{-(1-\kappa)/2}n^{-1/2}\) and is absorbed by the parametric floor.  If \(r_{1n}=0\), this nonparametric term is zero.

At \(\kappa=1\) we use exact sums, not a density argument.  Let \(s=(nr_{1n}^2)^{-1}\le s_0\), define
\[
J_s=\max\{j:t_j\ge s\},
\qquad K_s=J_s+1,
\qquad a_s=\frac{c_A}{\sqrt{nK_s}},
\]
and put \(g_{1,\pm}=\pm f\), where
\[
f=\frac{a_s}{e_0}\mathbf1\{s\le e_0\le s_0,\ \mathrm{active}\}. \tag{20}
\]
When \(\kappa=1\), (5) is \(w_j=(A/2)t_j\).  Since the active indices in (20) are \(j=0,\ldots,J_s\), exact geometric summation gives
\[
\begin{split}
\|f\|_2^2
 &=\frac{A a_s^2(2^{K_s}-1)}{2s_0}\asymp\frac{a_s^2}{s},\\
E[e_0f^2]&=\frac A2a_s^2K_s,
\qquad
E[f]=\frac A2a_sK_s.                                       
\end{split}                                                   \tag{21}
\]
The first line uses \(t_{J_s}\ge s>t_{J_s+1}\), hence \(2^{K_s}/s_0\asymp1/s\).  Substituting \(s=(nr_{1n}^2)^{-1}\) and \(a_s^2=c_A^2/(nK_s)\) yields
\[
\|f\|_2^2\le Cc_A^2r_{1n}^2,
\qquad
\operatorname{KL}(P_+^n,P_-^n)
=\frac{2n}{\sigma^2}E[e_0f^2]\le Cc_A^2,                    \tag{22}
\]
while the ATE separation is
\[
2E[f]=Aa_sK_s\asymp n^{-1/2}\sqrt{K_s}
\asymp n^{-1/2}\sqrt{1+\log_+(nr_{1n}^2)}.                  \tag{23}
\]
The last comparison has constants depending only on \(s_0\).  If \(s>s_0\), or if \(K_s\) is bounded, the last display is at most a fixed multiple of \(n^{-1/2}\), so the parametric experiment applies.  The observed second moment contributed by (20) is \(E[e_0f^2]=Ac_A^2/(2n)\), and the regression-radius and KL requirements have both been checked explicitly.  For \(\kappa>1\), def:tail-noise-rate gives \(Q_\kappa(n,r_{1n})=n^{-1/2}\).  Equations (16)--(23) therefore prove the entire \(Q_\kappa\) channel.

For the empty-treated-shell channel, choose \(s=c_s n^{-1/(\kappa+1)}\le s_0\), with fixed \(c_s>0\) sufficiently small, and use (17).  Couple the two samples identically unless some row both lies in \(A_s\) and is treated.  By a union bound and (8),
\[
\operatorname{TV}(P_+^n,P_-^n)
\le nP\{X\in A_s,D=1\}
\le Cns^{\kappa+1}=Cc_s^{\kappa+1}.                          \tag{24}
\]
Choose \(c_s\) so that this is at most \(1/4\).  By (7), the target separation is
\[
2hm_s\asymp r_{1n}s^{\kappa/2}
\asymp r_{1n}n^{-\kappa/[2(\kappa+1)]}.                     \tag{25}
\]
This family has signal norm \(c_A r_{1n}\) and observed regression contribution bounded by \(C c_A^2r_{1n}^2s\), so (15) applies.

For the treated nuisance-product channel, first suppose \(r_{en}>0\) and
\[
s=c_s r_{en}^{2/(\kappa+2)}\le s_0/2,
\qquad B_s=\{s<e_0\le2s,\ \mathrm{active}\},
\qquad m=P_X(B_s)\asymp s^\kappa,                            \tag{26}
\]
where (9) proves the last comparison.  Partition every active level in \(B_s\) into \(N\) equal subcells, and relabel their union as equal-mass cells, increasing \(N\) by at most a fixed factor if two levels occur.  Let independent signs satisfy
\[
\Pr_\theta(Z_j=z)=\frac{1+\theta\delta z}{2},
\qquad \theta,z\in\{-1,1\},
\qquad \delta=\frac14.                                     \tag{27}
\]
For each fixed \((\theta,Z)\), put on cell \(j\)
\[
g_1=hZ_j,\quad h=\frac{c_A r_{1n}}{\sqrt m},
\quad e_{\theta,Z}=\frac{e_0}{1+\theta\delta Z_j},
\quad m_1=0,\quad p=e_0,\quad g_0=m_0=0.                    \tag{28}
\]
The propensity ratio belongs to \([4/5,4/3]\).  Since \(e_0\le2s\le s_0<L/4\), positivity and right overlap follow, and (13)--(14) prove both shell inequalities for every fixed sign.  Also
\[
\|m_1-g_1\|_2=c_A r_{1n}\le r_{1n},
\qquad
\|p-e_{\theta,Z}\|_2
\le C\delta s\sqrt m
\le r_{en},                                                   \tag{29}
\]
because \(s\sqrt m\asymp s^{1+\kappa/2}=c_s^{1+\kappa/2}r_{en}\), and \(c_s\) is decreased if necessary.  The signal norm equals \(c_A r_{1n}\), and the observed outcome contribution is at most \(C c_A^2r_{1n}^2s\); thus (15) verifies the remaining moment conditions law by law.

For an observation in a cell not previously sampled,
\[
\Pr_\theta(Z_j=z)e_{\theta,z}
=\frac{1+\theta\delta z}{2}\frac{e_0}{1+\theta\delta z}
=\frac{e_0}{2}.                                               \tag{30}
\]
Thus the treated-row mixture, including the outcome \(hZ_j\), is independent of \(\theta\).  The control outcome is zero and
\[
\sum_{z=\pm1}\Pr_\theta(Z_j=z)(1-e_{\theta,z})
=\sum_{z=\pm1}\frac{1+\theta\delta z-e_0}{2}=1-e_0,          \tag{31}
\]
so the control-row mixture is also independent of \(\theta\).  Couple the two sample mixtures until two observations from \(B_s\) hit the same cell.  The union bound gives
\[
\operatorname{TV}(\overline P_+^n,\overline P_-^n)
\le\frac{n(n-1)m^2}{2N}\le\frac{n(n-1)}{2N}.                \tag{32}
\]
Under prior \(\theta\),
\[
\tau(P_{\theta,Z})=\frac{hm}{N}\sum_{j=1}^NZ_j,
\quad E_\theta\tau(P_{\theta,Z})=\theta\delta hm,
\quad \operatorname{Var}_\theta\{\tau(P_{\theta,Z})\}
\le\frac{h^2m^2}{N}.                                        \tag{33}
\]
Choose \(N\) larger than fixed multiples of \(n^2\) and \(\delta^{-2}\).  Then (32) and Chebyshev's inequality, obtained by applying Markov's inequality to the squared centered target, make respectively the mixture discrepancy and the probability of deviation by more than \(\delta hm/2\) at most \(1/16\).  The mixture form of (2) yields an obstruction of order
\[
hm\asymp r_{1n}s^{\kappa/2}
\asymp r_{1n}r_{en}^{\kappa/(\kappa+2)}.                    \tag{34}
\]
If the value in (26) exceeds \(s_0/2\), use the fixed active band at a scale below \(s_0\) and replace \(\delta\) by a small fixed multiple of \(\min\{r_{en}/\sqrt m,1\}\).  The same calculations give separation \(cr_{1n}\min\{r_{en},1\}\).  Since the large branch bounds \(r_{en}\) below by a positive class constant and \(r_{en}\le\bar r\), this dominates (34) up to a class constant.  If \(r_{en}=0\), the desired product is zero.

For the control nuisance product use the fixed band (10).  Divide it into its \(N\) equal cells and, for each fixed \((\theta,Z)\), set
\[
g_0=h_0Z_j,\quad h_0=\frac{c_A r_{0n}}{\sqrt{m_*}},
\quad m_0=0,\quad p=e_0,\quad g_1=m_1=0,
\quad
1-e_{\theta,Z}=\frac{1-e_0}{1+\theta tZ_j},                 \tag{35}
\]
where
\[
t=c_A\min\left\{\frac{r_{en}}{\sqrt{m_*}},\frac14\right\},
\qquad
\Pr_\theta(Z_j=z)=\frac{1+\theta tz}{2}.                   \tag{36}
\]
By (15), \(t\le c_A/4\le s_c/4\).  With \(b=\theta tZ_j\), direct algebra gives
\[
e_{\theta,Z}=\frac{e_0+b}{1+b},
\qquad
\frac{e_{\theta,Z}}{e_0}
=1+\frac{b(1-e_0)}{e_0(1+b)}.                               \tag{37}
\]
Since \(e_0>s_c\) and \(|b|\le s_c/4\),
\[
\frac34\le\frac{e_{\theta,Z}}{e_0}\le\frac54.             \tag{38}
\]
In particular \(e_0+b>3s_c/4>0\), proving positivity.  Also
\[
e_{\theta,Z}\le\frac54e_0\le\frac52s_c
<\frac54s_0<\frac5{16}L<L,                                  \tag{39}
\]
which proves right overlap.  Equations (13)--(14) apply to (38), so every fixed-sign control law satisfies both shell inequalities.

Furthermore,
\[
|e_{\theta,Z}-e_0|
=\frac{t(1-e_0)}{|1+b|}\le\frac{t}{1-t},
\qquad
\|e_{\theta,Z}-p\|_2\le\frac{t\sqrt{m_*}}{1-t}\le r_{en}. \tag{40}
\]
For the last inequality, in the first branch of (36) use \(c_A/(1-c_A/4)\le1\); in the second use \(r_{en}>\sqrt{m_*}/4\) and the same bound after the original uniform choice of \(c_A\).  Also
\[
\|g_0-m_0\|_2=h_0\sqrt{m_*}=c_A r_{0n}\le r_{0n}.           \tag{41}
\]
The signal norm is \(c_A r_{0n}\), the observed control outcome contribution is at most \(c_A^2r_{0n}^2\), and all residual variances are zero.  Equations (15), (38)--(41), and the causal construction therefore verify every condition defining \(\mathcal M_n\) for every fixed \((\theta,Z)\).

The mixture cancellation is exact.  Including the control outcome \(Y=h_0z\),
\[
\Pr_\theta(Z_j=z)(1-e_{\theta,z})
=\frac{1+\theta tz}{2}\frac{1-e_0}{1+\theta tz}
=\frac{1-e_0}{2}.                                            \tag{42}
\]
For a treated row, whose outcome is zero,
\[
\sum_{z=\pm1}\Pr_\theta(Z_j=z)e_{\theta,z}
=\sum_{z=\pm1}\frac{e_0+\theta tz}{2}=e_0.                 \tag{43}
\]
Thus unseen-cell one-row mixtures agree.  The collision coupling gives total variation at most \(n(n-1)m_*^2/(2N)\).  The random target has
\[
\tau(P_{\theta,Z})=-\frac{h_0m_*}{N}\sum_{j=1}^NZ_j,
\quad
E_\theta\tau(P_{\theta,Z})=-\theta th_0m_*,
\quad
\operatorname{Var}_\theta\{\tau(P_{\theta,Z})\}
\le\frac{h_0^2m_*^2}{N}.                                    \tag{44}
\]
Choose \(N\) larger than fixed multiples of \(n^2\) and \(t^{-2}\) when \(t>0\).  The collision and target-concentration errors are then at most \(1/16\), and the half-separation is
\[
d_0=th_0m_*
=c_A^2r_{0n}\min\{r_{en},\sqrt{m_*}/4\}.                    \tag{45}
\]
In the small branch this is \(c_A^2r_{0n}r_{en}\).  In the large branch, \(r_{en}>\sqrt{m_*}/4\) and \(r_{en}\le\bar r\), so
\[
d_0=\frac{c_A^2\sqrt{m_*}}4r_{0n}
\ge\frac{c_A^2\sqrt{m_*}}{4\bar r}r_{0n}r_{en}.            \tag{46}
\]
Equations (2) and (42)--(46) prove the \(r_{0n}r_{en}\) obstruction; if \(t=0\), that component is zero.

We have therefore produced fixed public inputs and fixed-sign laws in \(\mathcal M_n\) giving testing separations proportional to
\[
Q_\kappa(n,r_{1n}),\qquad
r_{1n}n^{-\kappa/[2(\kappa+1)]},\qquad
r_{1n}r_{en}^{\kappa/(\kappa+2)},\qquad
r_{0n}r_{en}.                                                 \tag{47}
\]
The first quantity includes the parametric alternative.  Since the sum of four nonnegative numbers is at most four times their maximum, (2), after taking the smallest positive testing constant across the four experiments, gives constants \(c>0\) and \(\delta_0\in(0,1/4)\), depending only on the fixed class constants, such that every \(T\in\mathcal T_n\) satisfies
\[
\sup_{(P,m_0,m_1,p)\in\mathcal M_n}
P\{|T-\tau(P)|\ge c\rho_n\}\ge\delta_0.                   \tag{48}
\]
The public functions and certified radii are identical inside each experiment, so allowing \(T\) to use them does not distinguish its hypotheses.  On the event in (48), absolute loss is at least \(c\rho_n\) and squared loss at least \(c^2\rho_n^2\).  Taking expectations, then suprema over \(\mathcal M_n\), and finally the infima in def:absolute-risk and def:root-mse-risk yields
\[
\mathfrak R_n^{(1)}\ge c\delta_0\rho_n,
\qquad
